title: Balancing refusal rates and attack success rates

opening.headline: If we've strengthened defense while reducing attacks, and even normal requests are being rejected, where should we set the defense intensity?
body: The security team reports that attacks have nearly disappeared after strengthening the filter. At the same time, customers complain that normal inquiries to the customer service center have been blocked. Both statements are true. This is because a single tuning mechanism for defense strength is simultaneously affecting both outcomes.

In this class, we verify what defense strength means through actual configurations, and examine how attack success rate and rejection rate move together according to the strength level. Then, we establish criteria for determining whether adjustments are appropriate, and demonstrate practice exercises for reading two indicators using two examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The defense strength and the relationship between the two indicators can be distinguished and analyzed.
It is possible to determine whether the defense strength adjustment is appropriate.

screens.title: After strengthening the defense, normal requests are being rejected.
screens.lead: Read the situation where the security team and the customer service team are telling different stories.

visual.alt: A diagram showing a single adjustment knob affecting both attack success rate and normal request rejection rate simultaneously.
labels: Security team: The attack has nearly disappeared
Customer Service: Normal inquiries are blocked

paragraphs: The security team strengthened the input filter. Reports indicate that attack attempts are now nearly being blocked. During the same week, customer service received complaints that ordinary inquiries were not being responded to. Neither report is incorrect.

The two reports originate from the same cause. Increasing the defense strength—a single control mechanism—reduces the attack success rate while simultaneously increasing the likelihood that normal requests will be blocked. To one observer, the defense appears successful; to another, it appears to have failed.

If strength is set to maximum, attacks are almost completely blocked but services become unusable. If strength is set to minimum, services function smoothly but attacks pass through. Therefore, the issue is not how strongly to block, but where to place the protection appropriately.
The question of this class is this: when viewing two indicators together, where should defensive strength be positioned?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If we place the security team's metrics and the customer service team's metrics side by side, which column should we add so both teams are discussing the same story?

screens.outro: First, let us recall your service.

screens.title: Review: Are we considering the rejection rate of normal requests?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please first think through the question on your own before entering an answer.

items.prompt: Are you measuring the rejection rate of normal requests?
items.answer: Many teams only track attack block counts and do not measure the rejection of legitimate requests. Without measurement, excessive defense measures remain hidden until user dissatisfaction accumulates.

items.prompt: Have you ever encountered a rejected normal request?
items.answer: Looking only at the numbers, we can only know the rejection rate percentage. By reading actual cases, we can see which expressions or topics are improperly blocked, and we gain clues about how to narrow down the rules.

items.prompt: Is there a way for users to report rejected requests?
items.answer: If there is no reporting pathway, the system silently removes the user. OpenAI's Safety Guidelines also advise providing users with easy ways to report issues. Reporting serves as a valuable source for normal request cases included in evaluation sets.

screens.outro: Now let's look at what the defense strength looks like in actual settings.

screens.title: What is defense strength?
screens.lead: Review how defense strength is represented by its set value in Gemini API's safety settings. You can check the meaning of each line and the symptoms when they mismatch in the right-side description.

notes.note: safety_settings is a list that pairs blocking thresholds by category. The categories are harassment, hate_speech, sexually_explicit, dangerous_content, and jailbreak, with one setting per category. For categories with insufficient configuration, the default value is used, and the default value for Gemini 2.5 and later models is off. If only one category is specified, the rest remain empty.

block_low_and_above is the most strict setting, starting from the lowest probability. If it's too strict, normal requests may be blocked and the rejection rate increases; if it's too lenient, the attack success rate rises.

block_only_high is a lenient setting that only blocks when the likelihood of unsafe behavior is high. The intermediate level is block_medium_and_above, and off disables the filter. There may be legitimate cases where, due to the nature of the service, certain categories are intentionally left lenient—similar to how game dialogue might allow for some flexibility.

The jailbreak category targets prompts aimed at bypassing safety filters. If this category is removed, defense against bypass attempts remains disabled by default, resulting in no reduction in the success rate of attacks in this range.

If a filter blocks input or output, the request fails with HTTP 400 and the error code becomes safety-related; the blocked content is not returned. Since this failure rate directly impacts the service's rejection rate, it must be included in the rejection rate aggregation.

screens.outro: Having read the configuration values, let's now observe how the two indicators change when the intensity is adjusted.

screens.title: Curves of two indicators based on defense strength
screens.lead: Try adjusting the defense strength using the slider. You can see how attack success rates and normal request rejection rates vary across different strength levels, and identify potential balance points. The values are hypothetical examples for illustrative purposes.

visual.alt: Two curve graphs showing that as defense strength increases, attack success rate decreases and normal request rejection rate increases.

stops.body: Example scenario: attack success rate of 12%, legitimate request denial rate of 1%. The filter is almost non-functional, allowing the service to be easily used but permitting many attacks to pass through. While we could say defense is enabled, it is difficult to claim that defense is effective. This state becomes the baseline for all subsequent comparisons.

Example scenario: Attack success rate is 5%, and normal request denial rate is 3%. When increasing the intensity, the attack success rate drops significantly, while the normal request denial rate slightly increases. In this range, the benefit of blocking attacks far outweighs the cost of increased normal request denials.

Example scenario: Attack success rate of 3%, normal request rejection rate of 9%. The attack success rate has decreased by 2 points, but the normal request rejection rate has increased by 6 points. In this range, the cost of mitigation becomes high. The segment where the curve bends—the "knee"—is a candidate for the balance point.

Example scenario: Attack success rate of 2.5%, normal request rejection rate of 30%. The attack success rate remains almost unchanged, but the rejection rate of normal requests has significantly increased. This makes the service difficult to use, achieving security at the expense of usability. The balance point varies depending on the risk the service can tolerate; therefore, medical consultations and internal document summaries are not placed at the same level.

screens.outro: Having observed the curve, I will now organize the criteria for determining the appropriate position.

screens.title: Criteria for determining whether adjustment is appropriate
screens.lead: When you select an item and expand it, you can view the criteria to verify whether the defense strength adjustment is appropriate. Please expand all of them.

items.title: Define success criteria in numerical terms
items.body: Ambiguous criteria like safe output cannot be judged to determine whether adjustments were appropriate. The Claude documentation advises to present the number stating that out of 10,000 instances, the output triggering content filtering due to toxicity is less than 0.1%. This numerical criterion allows verification of whether the intensity was properly adjusted afterward.

items.title: Look at the two indicators separately.
items.body: Separate attack requests from normal requests and examine both the attack success rate and the rejection rate of normal requests. Looking at only one aspect masks the damage on the other side. This judgment criterion serves as the starting point for finding the balance.

items.title: Compare using the same evaluation set
items.body: We evaluate both before and after strength changes using the same evaluation dataset for comparison. If the evaluation dataset differs, we wouldn't know whether the numerical difference stems from the strength change or from the data itself. This is why we record the evaluation dataset version.

items.title: Establish a reporting pathway.
items.body: Provides a pathway for users to report denied normal requests. This serves as a channel to identify undetected denials and acts as data to enhance the normal request evaluation dataset.

items.title: Combines with other means
items.body: We don't rely on a single strength factor to solve all problems. By combining various measures—such as input length restrictions, human review, login requirements, handling of repeated violators, and input filtering—we can reduce risks without drastically increasing security strength. Defense should be layered. By dividing defenses into layers, if one layer misses legitimate requests, another layer can compensate, and by keeping each layer's strength low, overall risk can be significantly reduced.

screens.outro: Having established the standard, let's apply it to the example.

screens.title: Explanation: When intensity is increased, reading the two indicators
screens.lead: After increasing the intensity, the instructor interprets the resulting number step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Numbers before and after change
steps.body: Before enhancement, the attack success rate was 12% and the rate of normal request rejection was 1%. After enhancement, the attack success rate dropped to 3% and the rate of normal request rejection increased to 9%. It is assumed that these figures are from the same evaluation set version.

steps.title: Convert to Differential
steps.body: The attack success rate decreased by 9 points, while the rejection rate for normal requests increased by 8 points. Since the increase offsets the decrease, the benefit gained is roughly equal to the cost incurred. Looking solely at the attack success rate, it dropped from 12% to 3%, appearing to have improved significantly.

steps.title: The practical meaning of numbers
steps.body: A 9% rejection rate for normal requests means that out of 100 normal inquiries, 9 are blocked. For a service receiving thousands of inquiries per day, this translates to hundreds of users being rejected without reason every day. Expressing this figure in terms of user count and request volume makes the cost tangible.

steps.title: Determine if it is manageable
steps.body: Judgment depends on the service characteristics. If the impact of an attack is extremely severe, accepting 9% inconvenience may be acceptable. Conversely, for services that support daily operations, such a level of inconvenience may be difficult to bear. The answer lies not in a number, but in the risk that the service itself can withstand.

steps.title: Response when unable to handle
steps.body: If it cannot be handled, reduce the strength by one level, and if defense decreases, address it with alternative methods. After reducing, re-evaluate using the same dataset to verify both metrics. This adjustment is not completed in one go; it is iterative and repeated by continuously monitoring the metrics.

screens.outro: In the following example, we will examine the vulnerabilities inherent in the configuration itself.

screens.title: Analysis: Reading a flawed configuration with medium strength and remediation measures
screens.lead: Select the excerpt indicated in the incident report below to view the instructor's interpretation. Verify how a configuration vulnerability manifests as a symptom in the indicator.

data.text: Incident configuration: [{"type": "hate_speech", "threshold": "block_low_and_above"}, {"type": "harassment", "threshold": "block_low_and_above"}]. Operational symptoms: Normal inquiries are accumulating at HTTP 400, code=safety, leading to an increasing rejection rate, yet The success rate of attacks in the hazardous content category has not decreased.. Recommended mitigation direction: Set thresholds according to service risk for each category, aiming for moderate intensity.. Remaining attacks: By limiting input length and repetition violations, the remaining overflow is reduced through narrowing the reporting path and rules..

marks.note: Both categories are set to the most stringent level. The most stringent setting could be the cause of blocking legitimate requests.

When filtering is blocked, it fails like this. Since this count is aggregated as a rejection rate, the fact that normal inquiries accumulate due to this error indicates that excessive defense is occurring.

marks.span: The success rate of attacks in the hazardous content category has not decreased.
marks.note: The dangerous_content, sexually_explicit, and jailbreak categories are not present in the settings, so these categories remain at their default off value. This serves as evidence that setting just one category strictly does not enhance the entire system.

marks.span: Set thresholds according to service risk for each category, aiming for moderate intensity.
marks.note: Assign values appropriate to the service risk for each category. For example, aim for a medium level of attack success rate of 5% and a normal request denial rate of 3%.

marks.span: By limiting input length and repetition violations, the remaining overflow is reduced through narrowing the reporting path and rules.
marks.note: This is a method that increases only the intensity without stacking layers. It reduces remaining attacks and remaining oger units using different means.

screens.outro: I will now summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the core of this course once again.

paragraphs: Security and usability lie on a single curve. Increasing defense strength reduces attack success rates but raises the rejection rate of legitimate requests. In the inflection point region of the curve, the gains are limited while the costs increase, making this area a candidate for a balance point.

The threshold is not a universal value but varies depending on the risk level that the service can withstand. When reviewing settings, you must verify whether a threshold has been specified for each category. Categories without thresholds will fall back to default values, creating vulnerabilities.

Strength is not a fixed value but one that is adjusted based on indicators. Set a success criterion as a number, compare the pre- and post-change performance on the same evaluation set, and combine it with other methods such as input constraints or human review.

In practice, it is important to develop the habit of showing both the attack success rate and the rejection rate of normal requests side by side in the report, rather than listing only the attack success rate. Having both numbers allows the security team and service owners to discuss based on the same evidence, preventing decisions to adjust severity from being biased toward one stakeholder group. Periodically reviewing examples of rejected normal requests also helps identify issues that are not immediately apparent from the numbers alone.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: When informed that the attack success rate has decreased, first inquire about how the rejection rate for normal requests has changed.

glossary.def: This is a tuning parameter that determines how strictly defenses are applied, similar to a blocking threshold.
The ratio of rejected requests. The rejection rate within normal requests indicates excessive defense.
The ratio of policy violation outputs that occurred during attack inputs.
This is the phase where the reduction of attack success rate begins to slow down and normal request rejection starts to increase.
A list of configured thresholds paired with each malicious category in the Gemini API. Most categories use default values.

misconceptions.myth: The higher the defense strength, the safer it is.
misconceptions.fact: Normal requests may be blocked, leading to a loss of service value. The benefits gained increase less as intensity increases, while the costs incurred rise.

misconceptions.myth: The balance point is the same in any service.
misconceptions.fact: It varies depending on the risks assumed by the service. Medical consultations and internal document summaries are not placed in the same location.

misconceptions.myth: Adjusting only the intensity is sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: Combining means and layers such as input restrictions, human review, and responses to repeated violations can reduce risks without drastically increasing intensity.

misconceptions.myth: Setting just one category strictly enhances the entire system.
misconceptions.fact: Each category has its own setting. For many categories, the default value is used, and since Gemini 2.5 onwards, the default is set to off, thus leaving potential vulnerabilities.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Security and usability exist on a curve.
Increasing defense strength decreases attack success rate and increases rejection rate.
The balance point is determined based on the risk level of the service.
Strength is adjusted based on indicators and combined with other means.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: The most difficult error to handle in our service is whether an attack is successfully passing through, or whether legitimate requests are being blocked? Is this judgment currently reflected in our current defense strength?

checks.q:
Which service behavior matches when only the following settings are applied?  
"safety_settings": [{"type": "hate_speech", "threshold": "block_low_and_above"}]
options: Hate speech is blocked with a low probability, while the remaining categories remain at the default value (off).
The remaining categories also inherit the same threshold and are strictly blocked accordingly.
Hate speech is only blocked with high probability; otherwise, it is moderate.
Since there is only one category, the entire configuration is rejected and all requests fail.
checks.explain: Each category has one setting, and for categories with insufficient settings, the default value is used. Since Gemini 2.5, the default value is off; therefore, specifying one category means the rest will be left empty.

wrong.1: Thresholds are applied separately by category and are not inherited.
wrong.2: block_low_and_above is the most strict option, starting from a low probability.
wrong.3: Specifying a single category is also a valid configuration.

checks.intro: Please check now how the settings you just read actually function. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Only a limited number of categories are applied, the rest use default values.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again about the scope within which settings are applied. The fact that settings are separate for each category is a clue.

checks.q: As a result of increasing strength, the attack success rate decreased from 12% to 3%, and the normal rejection rate increased from 1% to 9%. What is the most appropriate judgment?
options: Since the attack success rate has decreased, we maintain the changes as is.
Checks whether the service can handle 9 out of 100 normal requests being blocked.
The normal rejection rate is excluded from security assessments due to usability issues.
Increase the strength to maximum, setting the attack success rate to 0%.
checks.explain: Two indicators must be considered together. Determine whether it is within the service's inherent characteristics that 9% of normal requests are blocked; if not, reduce the intensity and employ alternative methods.

wrong.0: Looking at only the attack success rate misses the damage caused by normal requests.
wrong.2: The normal rejection rate is a key indicator for determining the balance point.
wrong.3: The maximum intensity increases normal rejection further and is inconsistent with a layer-by-layer approach.

checks.intro: Choose how to interpret the number after increasing the strength. The result is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Good judgment. You should analyze both indicators together to assess the feasibility of bearing the risk.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This is a judgment based on only one indicator. Also consider the costs on the normal request side.
